answer:
Tossing a fair coin repeatedly gives independent trials, each with the same two outcomes, so these are Bernoulli trials.

Let \(X\) denote the number of heads in 5 tosses. Then \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with

\(n = 5\), \(p = P(\text{head}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(q = 1 - p = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

The p.m.f. is

\(P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x}p^{x}q^{n-x} = \binom{5}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{5-x} = \dfrac{\binom{5}{x}}{2^{5}}\)

"Exactly three times head" means \(x = 3\):

\(P(X = 3) = \dfrac{\binom{5}{3}}{32} = \dfrac{10}{32} = \dfrac{5}{16}\)

using \(\binom{5}{3} = \dfrac{5 \times 4}{2 \times 1} = 10\).

\(\therefore\) the required probability is \(\dfrac{5}{16} = 0.3125\).
twin: If fair coin is tossed 10 times find the probability that it shows heads (i) 5 times.

answer:
The six operations are independent and each has the same recovery probability, so they are Bernoulli trials.

Let \(X\) denote the number of patients who recover. Then \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with

\(n = 6\), \(p = 0.5 = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(q = 1 - p = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(P(X = x) = \binom{6}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6-x} = \dfrac{\binom{6}{x}}{2^{6}} = \dfrac{\binom{6}{x}}{64}\)

**(i) None will recover** means \(x = 0\):

\(P(X = 0) = \dfrac{\binom{6}{0}}{64} = \dfrac{1}{64}\)

\(\therefore P(\text{none recovers}) = \dfrac{1}{64} = 0.0156\) (to 4 decimal places).

**(ii) Half of them will recover** means \(x = 3\), since half of 6 is 3:

\(P(X = 3) = \dfrac{\binom{6}{3}}{64} = \dfrac{20}{64} = \dfrac{5}{16}\)

using \(\binom{6}{3} = \dfrac{6 \times 5 \times 4}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 20\).

\(\therefore P(\text{half recover}) = \dfrac{5}{16} = 0.3125\).
twin: The probability that a bulb produced by a factory will fuse after 150 days of use is \(0 \cdot 05\). Find the probability that out of 5 such bulbs (i) none will fuse after 150 days of use.

answer:
The 10 bombs are dropped independently, each with the same probability of hitting, so these are Bernoulli trials.

Let \(X\) denote the number of bombs that hit the target. Then \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with

\(n = 10\), \(p = 0.8 = \dfrac{4}{5}\), \(q = 1 - p = 0.2 = \dfrac{1}{5}\)

\(P(X = x) = \binom{10}{x}\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{10-x}\)

"Exactly 4 will hit the target" means \(x = 4\):

\(P(X = 4) = \binom{10}{4}\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{6}\)

Now \(\binom{10}{4} = \dfrac{10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 210\), and

\(\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{6} = \dfrac{4^{4}}{5^{4}} \times \dfrac{1}{5^{6}} = \dfrac{256}{5^{10}} = \dfrac{256}{9765625}\)

\(\therefore P(X = 4) = 210 \times \dfrac{256}{9765625} = \dfrac{53760}{9765625} = \dfrac{10752}{1953125}\)

\(\therefore P(X = 4) = 0.0055\) (to 4 decimal places).

(The answer is small, and rightly so: with \(p = 0.8\) the expected number of hits is \(np = 8\), so only 4 hits is well below what the distribution favours.)
twin: Probability that bomb will hit target is \(0 \cdot 8\). Find the probability that out of 10 bombs dropped exactly 2 will miss the target.

answer:
Let \(X\) denote the number of heads in 6 tosses of a fair coin. The tosses are Bernoulli trials, so \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with

\(n = 6\), \(p = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(q = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(P(X = x) = \binom{6}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6-x} = \dfrac{\binom{6}{x}}{64}\)

**(a) Exactly 5 times**, i.e. \(x = 5\):

\(P(X = 5) = \dfrac{\binom{6}{5}}{64} = \dfrac{6}{64} = \dfrac{3}{32}\)

\(\therefore P(\text{exactly 5 heads}) = \dfrac{3}{32} = 0.09375\).

**(b) At least once**, i.e. \(x \geq 1\). Summing six terms is avoidable: use the complement, since "at least one head" is the opposite of "no head at all".

\(P(X \geq 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - \dfrac{\binom{6}{0}}{64} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{64} = \dfrac{63}{64}\)

\(\therefore P(\text{at least one head}) = \dfrac{63}{64} = 0.9844\) (to 4 decimal places).
twin: A die is thrown 6 times. If 'getting an odd number' is a success, find the probability of (i) 5 successes.

answer:
Let \(X\) denote the number of heads in 8 tosses of a fair coin. The tosses are Bernoulli trials, so \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with

\(n = 8\), \(p = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(q = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(P(X = x) = \binom{8}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{8-x} = \dfrac{\binom{8}{x}}{2^{8}} = \dfrac{\binom{8}{x}}{256}\)

**(i) It shows no head**, i.e. \(x = 0\):

\(P(X = 0) = \dfrac{\binom{8}{0}}{256} = \dfrac{1}{256}\)

\(\therefore P(\text{no head}) = \dfrac{1}{256} = 0.0039\) (to 4 decimal places).

**(ii) It shows a head at least once**, i.e. \(x \geq 1\). This is the complement of part (i):

\(P(X \geq 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{256} = \dfrac{255}{256}\)

\(\therefore P(\text{at least one head}) = \dfrac{255}{256} = 0.9961\) (to 4 decimal places).

(The two answers must add to 1, and \(\dfrac{1}{256} + \dfrac{255}{256} = 1\), which checks the pair.)

Let \(X\) denote the number of heads in 10 tosses of a fair coin. These are Bernoulli trials, so \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with

\(n = 10\), \(p = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(q = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(P(X = x) = \binom{10}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{10-x} = \dfrac{\binom{10}{x}}{2^{10}} = \dfrac{\binom{10}{x}}{1024}\)

"At most six heads" means \(X \leq 6\), i.e. \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\). That is seven terms, whereas the complement \(X \geq 7\) needs only four, so work with the complement:

\(P(X \leq 6) = 1 - P(X \geq 7) = 1 - \left[P(7) + P(8) + P(9) + P(10)\right]\)

\(= 1 - \dfrac{\binom{10}{7} + \binom{10}{8} + \binom{10}{9} + \binom{10}{10}}{1024}\)

Now \(\binom{10}{7} = 120\), \(\binom{10}{8} = 45\), \(\binom{10}{9} = 10\), \(\binom{10}{10} = 1\), and their sum is \(176\).

\(\therefore P(X \leq 6) = 1 - \dfrac{176}{1024} = \dfrac{848}{1024} = \dfrac{53}{64}\)

\(\therefore\) the probability of getting at most six heads is \(\dfrac{53}{64} = 0.8281\) (to 4 decimal places).

**Check by direct addition.** \(\binom{10}{0} + \binom{10}{1} + \cdots + \binom{10}{6} = 1 + 10 + 45 + 120 + 210 + 252 + 210 = 848\), giving \(\dfrac{848}{1024}\) as before.
twin: If a fair coin is tossed 10 times, find the probability of getting (i) exactly six heads (ii) at least six heads (iii) at most six heads

answer:
A die has three odd faces (1, 3, 5) out of six, so a single throw is a Bernoulli trial with

\(p = P(\text{odd number}) = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(q = 1 - p = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

The die is thrown 6 times independently, so if \(X\) is the number of successes then \(X \sim B\left(6, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) and

\(P(X = x) = \binom{6}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6-x} = \dfrac{\binom{6}{x}}{64}\)

"At least 5 successes" means \(X = 5\) or \(X = 6\):

\(P(X \geq 5) = P(X = 5) + P(X = 6) = \dfrac{\binom{6}{5}}{64} + \dfrac{\binom{6}{6}}{64} = \dfrac{6 + 1}{64} = \dfrac{7}{64}\)

\(\therefore\) the probability of at least 5 successes is \(\dfrac{7}{64} = 0.1094\) (to 4 decimal places).
twin: A die is thrown 6 times. If 'getting an odd number' is a success, find the probability of (ii) at least 5 successes.

answer:
A die has three odd faces (1, 3, 5) out of six, so each throw is a Bernoulli trial with

\(p = P(\text{odd number}) = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(q = 1 - p = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

The die is thrown 6 times independently, so if \(X\) is the number of successes then \(X \sim B\left(6, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) and

\(P(X = x) = \binom{6}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6-x} = \dfrac{\binom{6}{x}}{64}\)

For 5 successes take \(x = 5\):

\(P(X = 5) = \dfrac{\binom{6}{5}}{64} = \dfrac{6}{64} = \dfrac{3}{32}\)

\(\therefore\) the probability of 5 successes is \(\dfrac{3}{32} = 0.09375\).

(Note the wording: this asks for *exactly* 5 successes. "At least 5 successes" would add \(P(X = 6) = \frac{1}{64}\) and give \(\frac{7}{64}\).)
twin: A die is thrown 6 times. If 'getting an odd number' is a success, find the probability of (i) 5 successes.

answer:
A pack of 52 cards contains 13 spades. Because each card is replaced before the next is drawn, the five draws are independent and the success probability stays the same throughout, so these are Bernoulli trials with

\(p = P(\text{spade}) = \dfrac{13}{52} = \dfrac{1}{4}\), \(q = 1 - p = \dfrac{3}{4}\)

Let \(X\) denote the number of spades drawn. Then \(X \sim B\left(5, \dfrac{1}{4}\right)\) and

\(P(X = x) = \binom{5}{x}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{5-x}\)

**(i) All the five cards are spades**, i.e. \(x = 5\):

\(P(X = 5) = \binom{5}{5}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{5}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{0} = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{5} = \dfrac{1}{1024}\)

\(\therefore P(\text{all five spades}) = \dfrac{1}{1024} = 0.0010\) (to 4 decimal places).

**(ii) None is a spade**, i.e. \(x = 0\):

\(P(X = 0) = \binom{5}{0}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{0}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{5} = \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{5} = \dfrac{243}{1024}\)

\(\therefore P(\text{none is a spade}) = \dfrac{243}{1024} = 0.2373\) (to 4 decimal places).

(Replacement is what makes this binomial. Drawing without replacement would change \(p\) at every draw and the model would be hypergeometric instead.)
twin: Five cards are drawn successively with replacement from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. find the probability that (i) all the five cards are spades. / (iii) none is a spade.

answer:
Given \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with \(E(X) = 6\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4.2\).

For a binomial distribution,

\(E(X) = np\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = npq\)

\(\therefore np = 6\) ... (1) and \(npq = 4.2\) ... (2)

**Find \(q\) by dividing**, which eliminates both unknowns at once:

\(\dfrac{npq}{np} = \dfrac{4.2}{6}\)

\(\therefore q = 0.7\)

**Hence \(p\).**

\(p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3\)

**Hence \(n\), from (1).**

\(n \times 0.3 = 6\)

\(\therefore n = \dfrac{6}{0.3} = 20\)

\(\therefore n = 20\) and \(p = 0.3\).

**Check.** \(np = 20 \times 0.3 = 6\) and \(npq = 20 \times 0.3 \times 0.7 = 4.2\), so both given values are reproduced. (Note also that \(q < 1\), as it must be: for a binomial distribution the variance is always less than the mean, since \(\mathrm{Var} = \mathrm{Mean} \times q\).)

Given \(X \sim B(n, p)\) with \(n = 10\) and \(E(X) = 5\).

For a binomial distribution the mean is

\(E(X) = np\)

Substituting the given values:

\(10p = 5\)

\(\therefore p = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5\)

\(\therefore p = 0.5\).

(Then \(q = 1 - p = 0.5\), and the variance would be \(npq = 10 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 2.5\), though only \(p\) was asked for.)
twin: Let \(X \sim B(n, p)\) (i) If \(n = 10\), \(E(X) = 5\), find \(p\) and \(Var(X)\).

answer:
**(A)**

The p.m.f. is \(P(X = x) = \binom{4}{x}\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right)^{x}\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^{4-x}\) for \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\).

**Recognise the distribution.** Compare with the binomial p.m.f. \(P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x}p^{x}q^{n-x}\). Matching term by term:

\(n = 4\), \(p = \dfrac{5}{9}\), \(q = \dfrac{4}{9}\)

and \(p + q = \dfrac{5}{9} + \dfrac{4}{9} = 1\), which confirms the identification. So \(X \sim B\left(4, \dfrac{5}{9}\right)\).

**Hence the mean.**

\(E(X) = np = 4 \times \dfrac{5}{9} = \dfrac{20}{9}\)

\(\therefore E(X) = \dfrac{20}{9}\), which is option (A).

**Why the others fail.** Option (B), \(\dfrac{9}{20}\), is the reciprocal of the correct answer. A single sanity check disposes of all three wrong options at once: \(X\) counts successes in 4 trials with \(p = \dfrac{5}{9} > \dfrac{1}{2}\), so the mean must exceed \(4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 2\). But \(\dfrac{9}{20} = 0.45\), \(\dfrac{12}{9} = 1.33\) and \(\dfrac{9}{25} = 0.36\) are all below 2, while \(\dfrac{20}{9} = 2.22\) is not.
twin: Let the p.m.f. of r.v. \(X\) be \(P(X = x) = {}^{4}C_{x}\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right)^{x} \times \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^{4-x}\), for \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\). Then find \(E(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\).

For a binomial distribution \(B(n, p)\),

mean \(= np\) and variance \(= npq\)

Given \(np = 18\) ... (1) and \(npq = 12\) ... (2)

**Divide (2) by (1)** to eliminate \(n\) and \(p\) together:

\(\dfrac{npq}{np} = \dfrac{12}{18}\)

\(\therefore q = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

**Hence \(p\).**

answer:
**(B)**

For a binomial distribution \(B(n, p)\),

mean \(= np\) and variance \(= npq\), where \(q = 1 - p\)

Given \(np = 18\) ... (1) and \(npq = 12\) ... (2)

**Divide (2) by (1),** which removes \(n\) and \(p\) in one step and leaves \(q\) alone:

\(\dfrac{npq}{np} = \dfrac{12}{18}\)

\(\therefore q = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

**Hence \(p\).**

\(p = 1 - q = 1 - \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)

**Hence \(n\), from (1).**

\(n \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 18\)

\(\therefore n = 54\), which is option (B).

**Check.** With \(n = 54\), \(p = \dfrac{1}{3}\), \(q = \dfrac{2}{3}\): \(np = 18\) and \(npq = 54 \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 12\), matching both given quantities.

(A useful shortcut for this standard type: \(q = \dfrac{\text{variance}}{\text{mean}}\), and then \(n = \dfrac{\text{mean}}{1 - q}\).)

answer:
Two dice are thrown. Let \(X\) denote the number of sixes obtained.

**Reading of the question.** \(X\) counts how many of the two dice show a six, so \(X\) can be \(0\), \(1\) or \(2\). (This is different from the event "a six appears on at least one die", which is a single event about the pair and would give a variable taking only the values 0 and 1. Here the question says "the number of sixes", so all three values are in play.)

Each die is an independent Bernoulli trial with

\(p = P(\text{six}) = \dfrac{1}{6}\), \(q = 1 - p = \dfrac{5}{6}\)

so \(X \sim B\left(2, \dfrac{1}{6}\right)\).

**Expectation by the binomial formula.**

\(E(X) = np = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)

\(\therefore E(X) = \dfrac{1}{3}\)

**Check from the distribution itself.** There are \(6 \times 6 = 36\) equally likely ordered outcomes:

\(P(X = 0) = \dfrac{5}{6} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{25}{36}\), \(P(X = 1) = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{10}{36}\), \(P(X = 2) = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{36}\)

| \(x_{i}\) | 0 | 1 | 2 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(p_{i}\) | \(\dfrac{25}{36}\) | \(\dfrac{10}{36}\) | \(\dfrac{1}{36}\) | 1 |
| \(x_{i}p_{i}\) | 0 | \(\dfrac{10}{36}\) | \(\dfrac{2}{36}\) | \(\dfrac{12}{36}\) |

\(E(X) = \sum x_{i}p_{i} = \dfrac{12}{36} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), agreeing with \(np\).

\(\therefore\) the expectation of the number of sixes is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\).
twin: Two dice are thrown simultaneously. If \(X\) denotes the number of sixes, find the expectation of \(X\).

answer:
Three coins are tossed simultaneously and \(X\) is the number of heads.

Each coin is an independent Bernoulli trial with \(p = P(\text{head}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(q = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so

\(X \sim B\left(3, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\), with \(n = 3\)

**Expected value.**

\(E(X) = np = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5\)

**Variance.**

\(\mathrm{Var}(X) = npq = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75\)

**Check from the distribution itself.** The sample space is

\(S = \{HHH,\ HHT,\ HTH,\ THH,\ HTT,\ THT,\ TTH,\ TTT\}\), so \(n(S) = 8\)

| \(x_{i}\) | \(p_{i}\) | \(x_{i}p_{i}\) | \(x_{i}^{2}p_{i}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | \(\dfrac{1}{8}\) | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) | \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) | \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) |
| 2 | \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) | \(\dfrac{6}{8}\) | \(\dfrac{12}{8}\) |
| 3 | \(\dfrac{1}{8}\) | \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) | \(\dfrac{9}{8}\) |
| **Total** | 1 | \(\dfrac{12}{8}\) | \(\dfrac{24}{8}\) |

\(E(X) = \dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = E\left(X^{2}\right) - \left[E(X)\right]^{2} = 3 - (1.5)^{2} = 3 - 2.25 = 0.75\)

Both agree with the \(np\) and \(npq\) values.

\(\therefore E(X) = 1.5\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = 0.75\).
twin: Three coins are tossed simultaneously, \(X\) is the number of heads. Find expected value and variance of \(X\).
